```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import glob
import re
import statistics
import pandas as pd
from _outils import *          # noqa: F403
# Load the constants and then the functions into the same namespace, rather than
# copying the values here: MARK and REDACTION stay defined in one single place.
ns = {"re": re}
for nom in ("MARK", "REDACTION", "protect", "restore", "sentences"):
    exec(compile(source_de(nom, PARAGRAPHES), "<traduire_paragraphes>", "exec"), ns)
protect, restore, sentences = ns["protect"], ns["restore"], ns["sentences"]
```

*Code covered: `protect`, `restore` and `sentences` in
`tools/traduire_paragraphes.py`.*

## What `___` is, and why it is the most fragile content

MIMIC-IV-Note is de-identified: dates, names, ages, places and numbers have been
replaced by a run of underscores.

```{python}
#| echo: false
notes = pd.read_excel(RACINE / "CATH-LLM" / "exampleNotes_250.xlsx")[["id_note", "input"]]
compte = notes.input.str.count("___")
print(f"redactions per note: median {compte.median():.0f}, min {compte.min()}, "
      f"max {compte.max()}")
print(f"total over the 249 notes: {compte.sum()}")
```

They have to cross the translation **intact and in place**. Two reasons:

1. comparing two languages assumes identical content. A lost redaction is a difference
   in content, and therefore a confounding variable in the measurement;
2. an *invented* redaction is worse: it manufactures missing data where the note had
   text. It happened during the manual translation — `PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: per AJ
   records` had become `prema dokumentaciji ___`.

And a translation model has no reason whatsoever to respect a run of underscores. It
may reformat it, merge two of them, move one, or drop one — and above all, **it does so
without an error**. Nothing in the output signals the loss.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The trap that does not get discussed enough

`___` does not always stand in for an identifier. Sometimes it stands in for **a
connecting word** in the middle of a sentence: `from LAD ___ gastric Lymphoma`,
`jaundice in the past ___ extrinsic compression`.

The temptation, for a model as much as for a human translator, is to translate the
*meaning* of the sentence and make the redaction disappear. On the contrary, one has to
write `limfadenopatijom ___ limfom želuca`, even at the cost of an awkward sentence: the
source is awkward too.
:::

This is the **only** concession `traduire_paragraphes.py` makes to the corpus format,
and it can be switched off with `--no-protect`. On a text without redactions it does
nothing anyway.

## `protect`: turning a fragile pattern into a robust one {#sec-protect}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("MARK", "REDACTION", "protect", ou=PARAGRAPHES)
```

Every redaction becomes a **unique integer**: 77701, 77702, 77703…

The reasoning fits in one sentence: *a translation model copies numbers faithfully,
because that is its job*. A date, a dosage, a laboratory result have to cross the
translation unchanged — models are trained for that. A run of underscores is not: it is
not language, and nothing protects it.

```{python}
extract = "The patient is a ___ year old woman. Catheter placed on ___ by Dr. ___."
p, n = protect(extract)
print("before :", extract)
print("after  :", p)
print("count  :", n)
```

Two details that matter:

- **the numbering is increasing and unique**, via the `nonlocal n` closure. Identical
  markers would make it impossible to check that none had been merged;
- **the count `n` is returned along with the text.** That is what makes the later check
  possible; without it, the source would have to be re-read.

The choice of 77700 as the base is not arbitrary: it is a five-digit number that has no
reason to appear in a discharge summary — laboratory values, blood pressures, doses and
years all live below it. It makes the control pattern `777\d\d` safe.

## `restore`: forgiving, and why that is the right trade-off

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("restore", ou=PARAGRAPHES)
```

The function puts back what comes back, counts what is missing, and converts any
residual marker — a `777xx` left as-is would be read as a clinical value, which would be
worse than giving it back.

```{python}
cases = [
    ("77701 year old woman, catheter placed 77702 by Dr. 77703.", "everything came back"),
    ("Woman in her 77701s, catheter placed by Dr. 77703.",        "77702 lost"),
    ("77701 year old, catheter 77702, Dr. 77702.",                "77703 became a duplicate"),
]
for output, description in cases:
    text, lost = restore(output, 3)
    print(f"  {description:26s} -> {lost} lost | {text}")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Whether to reject or tolerate depends on the size of the unit

An earlier version of this function rejected the output wholesale as soon as one marker
was missing, and the caller then kept the untranslated source text. That was not a
mistake: on a 90-character unit, replacing the translation with its source costs one
sentence and makes the failure visible.

The same trade-off becomes absurd as soon as the unit grows. On a paragraph — and *a
fortiori* on a 10,000-character note — a single missing marker would throw away all the
rest of the translation, which is good. Hence the opposite choice here: **restore what
comes back and quantify the loss**, rather than cancelling everything.

The general rule: the bigger the unit, the more wholesale rejection costs, and the more
it has to be replaced by a measurement.
:::

The `markers_lost` counter carries exactly that risk, note by note:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
lignes = []
for motif, nom in [("notes_retour_anglais.csv", "back HR -> EN"),
                   ("notes_croate_paragraphes.csv", "out EN -> HR")]:
    fs = glob.glob(str(RACINE / "results" / motif))
    if not fs:
        continue
    d = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in fs]).drop_duplicates("id_note")
    lignes.append({"corpus": nom, "notes": f"{len(d)}/249",
                   "source redactions": int(d.redactions_src.sum()),
                   "markers lost": int(d.markers_lost.sum()),
                   "rate": f"{d.markers_lost.sum() / max(1, d.redactions_src.sum()):.1%}"})
tableau(lignes) if lignes else print("*(no corpus produced yet)*")
```

## The `str.count("___")` counter over-counts

The simplest check is arithmetic: as many `___` on both sides. It fits on one line and
catches the dangerous failure mode. But it has a bias that has to be known in order to
read its signal.

```{python}
series = "Murmur [] grade ______ Abdomen: Soft"
p, n = protect(series)
back, _ = restore(p, n)
print(f"source   : {series!r}")
print(f"           count('___') = {series.count('___')}   (but one single redaction)")
print(f"protected: {p!r}   -> n = {n}")
print(f"restored : count('___') = {back.count('___')}")
```

`REDACTION = r"_{3,}"` treats a run of six underscores as **one** redaction, and gives
it back in its canonical form `___`. But `str.count("___")` counted two of them in the
source. The content is intact; it was the counter that was too generous.

::: {.callout-note}
## An imperfect check beats no check

This could be fixed by counting `len(REDACTION.findall(t))`. That would be more
accurate, and it would be a regression: the approximate count **over-reacts**, it flags
healthy notes. A check that rings for nothing costs ten minutes of reading; a check
that fails to ring when it should costs a corpus.

What matters, then, is knowing how to read the signal: a gap of 1 or 2 on a note
containing long runs is an artefact, a clear gap is a loss.
:::

## `sentences`: splitting a paragraph above the ceiling

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("sentences", ou=PARAGRAPHES)
```

96 % of paragraphs fit under 1,000 characters and therefore pass through whole. For the
rest, the only acceptable boundary is the end of a sentence: **a truncated sentence
yields a wrong translation, not merely an incomplete one.**

```{python}
text = ("Patient admitted with fever. Blood cultures were drawn from the line. "
        "The catheter was removed on day three. She improved on vancomycin.")
for i, m in enumerate(sentences(text, 80)):
    print(f"  [{i}] {len(m):3d} chars  {m}")
```

`re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text)` cuts *after* the punctuation: `(?<=…)` is a
lookbehind, so the separator consumed is the space and the full stop stays attached to
the sentence before it.

### What the function cannot do

```{python}
no_punctuation = "___ 05:30AM BLOOD WBC-12.3* RBC-3.64* " * 40
m = sentences(no_punctuation, 1000)
print(f"{len(no_punctuation)} chars -> {len(m)} piece(s), "
      f"longest {max(len(x) for x in m)} chars")
```

A block of laboratory values has no sentence-ending punctuation: the function cannot
split it and returns it whole. That is not a defect but a limit worth knowing — it is
for cases like this that `budget()` computes the generation ceiling per batch instead of
fixing it once and for all.

## The check before spending any GPU

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fichier(PARAGRAPHES, "    # Check the splitting before spending any GPU",
        "    plan_vram(")
```

With no translation involved, splitting then re-joining has to preserve every redaction.
The check costs two seconds and, were it to fail, would invalidate a run of several
hours.

## Takeaways

- The `___` redactions are the most fragile content in the corpus and the most silently
  lost; this whole chapter exists for them.
- `protect` converts them into integers because a translator copies numbers faithfully —
  it exploits a property of the model rather than working around it.
- `restore` tolerates and **quantifies** instead of rejecting: on a unit the size of a
  paragraph, wholesale rejection would throw away a correct translation over one marker.
- The `count("___")` check over-counts long runs. Keeping it as-is is a choice: a false
  alarm beats silence.
- `sentences` never cuts in the middle of a sentence, and cannot split a text without
  punctuation.
